text:
#### Initial Treatment Recommendations for Asthma-COPD Overlap

**For Patients with Predominant Asthma Characteristics:**
* **Corticosteroids:** Prescribe inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) to manage inflammation. It is important to note that long-acting bronchodilators should not be used as monotherapy in these cases.

**For Patients with Predominant COPD Symptoms:**
* **Bronchodilators:** Initiate treatment with appropriate long-acting bronchodilators to relieve symptoms.
* **Combination Therapy:** Consider a combination of ICS and long-acting bronchodilators for enhanced therapeutic effect. However, ICS should not be prescribed as monotherapy for COPD management.

These recommendations aim to optimize clinical efficacy and safety, ensuring that treatment is aligned with the patient’s specific clinical presentation.

text:
### **Diagnosis and Management of Bronchiectasis**

| Category | Management |
| --- | --- |
| **Non-Pharmacologic** | Postural drainage (e.g., lie head down 10–20 min ×3/day), Adequate hydration, Supplemental |
| **Therapy** | Oxygen, Patient education & preventive care |
| **Acute Care** | Antibiotics guided by Gram stain; target common pathogens (H. influenzae, P. aeruginosa if unknown), Bronchodilators if bronchospasm present |
| **Chronic Therapy** | Avoid tobacco, Maintain nutrition & hydration, Prompt treatment of infections, Vaccination (pneumococcal, influenza) |
| **Referral** | Consider partial lung resection for severe cases unresponsive to medical therapy |

If it is in keeping with bronchiectasis, bronchiectasis is confirmed. If not, request a thin-slice or high-resolution CT chest; if in keeping, confirmed; if not, consider an alternative diagnosis. Once confirmed, do routine tests (FBC, urea and creatinine, LFTs, glucose, HIV, sputum culture and TB culture, with Aspergillus IgE and sweat chloride) and further tests guided by history and examination (immunoglobulins, total IgE, nasal or bronchial biopsy). narrative: Management of microscopic haematuria (NCDIMH guidelines, page 349). Confirm red blood cells (more than 3 per high-power field) in 2 of 3 samples. If there are signs or symptoms of infection (dysuria, frequency, flank pain, leukocyte esterase, nitrites, white cells, bacteria), treat the infection and confirm resolution with urinalysis 6 weeks after therapy. If not, look for a glomerular cause (proteinuria, raised creatinine, red cell casts, dysmorphic red cells, abnormal sediment or reduced renal function); if present, refer to a nephrologist; cytology is a poor screening test and is not recommended initially. If another cause is probable (vigorous exercise, urethral trauma, menstruation, offending medication), retest urine after the factor is stopped. Otherwise do radiographic evaluation of the urinary tract (renal ultrasound, CT or intravenous pyelogram; if imaging is not available, refer to a urologist). After CT: if negative, do urine cytology; if positive, refer to a urology subspecialist. Negative findings in low-risk patients (under 40, no risk factors): follow up with urinalysis and blood pressure; if haematuria persists more than 3 months, consider specialist referral. Positive findings, all patients over 40, or younger patients with risk factors for urothelial tumours: refer to urology for cystoscopy.

text:
## **Standard Classification of Benign Prostatic Uropathy**

| Term | Full Name |  | Definition | Key Characteristics |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| BOO | Bladder | Outlet Obstruction | A generic clinical term for a blockage that slows or stops urine flow during voiding. | Diagnosed via urodynamics (shows high bladder pressure but low flow). |
| BPH | Benign | Prostatic Hyperplasia | A histological (microscopic) diagnosis referring to the overgrowth of prostate cells. | It is a cellular diagnosis, typically confirmed through biopsy or pathology after surgery. |
| BPE | Benign | Prostatic Enlargement | A clinical observation of an increased prostate volume (size), regardless of symptoms. | Can be detected via physical exam (Digital Rectal Exam) or imaging (Ultrasound). |
| BPO | Benign | Prostatic Obstruction | A specific form of BOO where the blockage is proven to be caused by BPE. | This links the physical size of the prostate to the actual obstruction of urine. |

### **Benign Prostatic Obstructive Uropathy** | **Line of** Therapy | **Indications** | **Interventions** | **Key Notes / Side Effects** | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | First-Line Therapy | BPE without bothersome symptoms - Mild IPSS score | Watchful Waiting (Mild IPSS): Reassure, reinforce healthy lifestyle | Education and lifestyle modification are central | | First-Line Therapy | Mild-Moderate IPSS | Urotherapy: Double voiding
• Treat constipation
• Bladder training
• Urethral milking post-void
• Control fluid intake (storage LUTS) | | | First-Line Therapy | Mild-Moderate IPSS | • Avoid bladder irritants (coffee, alcohol, cola, spicy foods)
• Optimise DM/HTN control if concomitant
• Substitute LUTS-exacerbating drugs (diuretics, TCAs, antihistamines, flu medications) | | | Second-Line Therapy | Moderate-severe LUTS - Failed 1st-line therapy | Alpha-1 Blockers - Relax internal sphincter & prostate smooth muscles | | | Second-Line Therapy | Preferred in normotensive patients | Tamsulosin / Uromax 0.4 mg OD (may double in selected cases) - Uroselective | • Retrograde ejaculation → ↓ ejaculate volume
• Orthostatic hypotension (first few weeks) → ↑ fall risk
• Floppy iris syndrome in cataract surgery → avoid in cataract patients | | Second-Line Therapy | Particularly useful in patients with hypertension | Doxazosin / Cardura 4 mg / 8 mg XL nocte | • Dizziness
• Asthenia
• Orthostatic hypotension
• Strong vasodilatory effect → avoid with nitrates or CCF |

narrative: Primary care management of erectile dysfunction (NCDIMH guidelines, page 354). The general practitioner does an initial assessment (sexual history, relevant blood tests, blood pressure, genital examination). A young patient with a history of trauma or penile or testicular abnormalities should be referred to urology immediately. Suggestive of psychogenic cause: sudden onset, good morning or self-stimulated erections, relationship problems, variable with circumstances; give first-line PDE5 inhibitors, monitor response, consider counselling. Suggestive of organic cause: gradual onset, lack of tumescence, normal libido, relevant medical history, smoking, difficulty with penetration; investigate (BMI, BP, abdominal circumference, HbA1c, lipids, encourage weight loss) and, for features of hypogonadism, check testosterone before 10 am, and if low, FSH, LH, prolactin and SHBG and thyroid function. If abnormal, refer to urology or endocrinology. If normal with no evidence of coronary heart disease (CHD), give PDE5 inhibitors. If normal but with CHD, get guidance from cardiology or medicine and consider PDE5 inhibitors once the patient is at low cardiac risk. PDE5 inhibitors: sildenafil, tadalafil (consider daily dose), vardenafil.

## How to measure blood pressure correctly

**Checklist:**
- No exercise, smoking, caffeine or food 30 min before
- Quiet environment
- Comfortable temperature
- 3-5 min rest before measurement
- No talking before or during measurements
- Take 3 measurements at 1 min intervals and use the average of the last two

### **Categories of Hypertension**

* Normal: below 90th percentile.
* Elevated Blood Pressure: 90th–95th percentile or BP >120/80 mmHg.
* Stage 1 Hypertension: >95th–99th percentile plus 12 mmHg.
  \*\*\*In adolescents if BP >140/90 mmHg, even <95th percentile
* Stage 2 Hypertension: >99th percentile plus 5 mmHg.

## <u>Pharmacological Management</u>

Treatment paradigms are conventionally based on the morphological type and severity of psoriasis. Starting with topical agents followed by phototherapy and then systemic agents is recommended. First line systemic therapy is indicated if topical therapy is impractical.

text:
# TERMINOLOGY

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Adverse Drug Reaction (ADR): | A response to a drug which is noxious and unintended, and which occurs at doses normally used in humans for prophylaxis, diagnosis, or therapy of disease, or for the modification of physiological function. An adverse drug reaction, in contrast to an adverse event, is characterized by the fact that a causal relationship between a medical product and an occurrence is suspected. |
| Adverse Event (AE)/Adverse Experience: | Any untoward medical occurrence that may present during treatment with a pharmaceutical product, but which does not necessarily have a causal relationship with this treatment. |
| Assigned female at birth: | People assigned female at birth may include cisgender women, transgender men, and some non-binary people. |
| Assigned male at birth: | People assigned male at birth may include cisgender men, transgender women, and some non-binary people. |
| Cisgender: | Describes a person whose gender identity corresponds to their sex assigned at birth. |
| Integration: | Joining operational programs to ensure effective outcomes through many modalities (multi-tasked providers, referral, one-stop-shop services under one roof, etc.) |
| Non-binary: | A spectrum of gender identities that do not exclusively or neatly fit into the category male or female, man or woman, and are outside the gender binary. |
| Transgender: | A person who has a gender identity or gender expression that differs from the sex assigned at birth. |
| Transgender woman: | An individual assigned male sex at birth who identifies as a female. |
| Transgender man: | An individual assigned female sex at birth who identifies as a male. |

text:
| Box 3. Ring insertion steps for clients |
| --- |
| 1. Get into a position that is comfortable for inserting the ring, such as squatting, one leg lifted, or lying down. If a health care provider is assisting you, you should be in a reclining position. |
| 2. With clean hands, squeeze the ring between the thumb and forefinger, pressing both sides of the ring together so that the ring forms a "figure 8" shape. |
| 3. Use the other hand to open the folds of skin around the vagina. |
| 4. Place the tip of the ring into the vaginal opening and use your fingers to push the folded ring gently up into the vagina. |

narrative: PrEP initiation decision pathway: HIV exposure and acute HIV infection (AHI) assessment (Figure 11). First ask whether the client's HIV test result is negative. If not negative, refer the client to confirmatory testing and HIV treatment. If negative, ask whether the client was potentially exposed to HIV in the past 72 hours. If yes, start post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) standard of care (SOC); if PEP is started, retest for HIV in 28 days, and if the client is seronegative on PEP completion, continue PrEP SOC. If no exposure in the past 72 hours, ask whether the client has AHI symptoms now or had them in the past 14 days. If no AHI symptoms, start PrEP SOC. If yes, ask whether there was a potential exposure in the 14 days before symptom onset. If no such exposure, start PrEP SOC. If yes, the symptoms may be due to AHI because a prevention method was not used effectively around the exposure; provider and client should weigh the risks and benefits of delaying PrEP initiation and retesting 28 days after the potential exposure, or earlier if testing that reliably detects HIV is available.

<sup>0</sup> An answer of “NO” to this question means no potential past exposure to HIV at all or potential HIV exposure was 72 or more hours ago.

<sup>1</sup> Two-thirds of people will have symptoms of AHI within two to four weeks of HIV acquisition. Signs/symptoms mimicking acute HIV infection (sore throat, fever, sweats, swollen glands, mouth ulcers, headache, rash, and muscle aches) are commonly due to illnesses other than HIV; providers need to use discretion in determining whether the symptomatology is consistent with HIV or may be explained by an alternative cause.

<sup>2</sup> In order to make informed choice prior to starting PrEP, the client should be aware that available HIV testing may not have been able to detect HIV if the client acquired HIV fewer than 28 days ago, and that there is a possibility the HIV test may not have detected

HIV if acquired beyond 28 days ago. The client should also be aware that while they do not have symptoms of AHI, they could be pre-symptomatic or be part of the one-third of individuals who do not develop symptoms of AHI within two to four weeks of acquiring HIV.

testing | ▪ Unavailability of or access to hepatitis B testing **should not be
a barrier** to PrEP initiation or use regardless of the method
choice. | | | ▪ Testing (oral PrEP users for hepatitis B at or within three months of PrEP initiation is strongly suggested where feasible.
▪ All recommended PrEP options can be safely offered to people with hepatitis B, so awaiting hepatitis B test results should not delay initiation.
▪ If tested for hepatitis B, clients who are negative can be offered hepatitis B vaccination (as per national treatment guidelines).
▪ Clients with hepatitis B who are not interested in oral PrEP should be referred to relevant management/treatment services.

narrative: PrEP follow-up decision pathway: HIV exposure, acute HIV infection (AHI) and effective-use assessment (Figure 12). First ask whether the client's HIV test result is negative. If not negative, refer to confirmatory testing and HIV treatment. If negative, ask whether there was a potential exposure to HIV in the past 72 hours. If yes, ask whether the client practiced effective use of their chosen prevention method during the exposure: if yes, continue PrEP standard of care (SOC); if no, start PEP SOC, retest for HIV in 28 days, and if seronegative on PEP completion continue PrEP SOC. If no exposure in the past 72 hours, ask whether the client has or had AHI symptoms in the past 14 days. If no symptoms, continue PrEP SOC; special effective-use counseling may be beneficial. If symptoms, ask whether there was a potential exposure in the 14 days before symptom onset. If no, symptoms are unlikely to be AHI because exposure and symptom timing do not align; continue PrEP SOC using best clinical judgement. If yes, ask whether the client used the prevention method effectively around that exposure. If yes, symptoms are unlikely to be AHI; continue PrEP SOC using best clinical judgement. If no, symptoms may be due to AHI; provider and client should weigh the risks and benefits of pausing PrEP and retesting 28 days from the exposure, or earlier if reliable testing is available.

text:
#### **Box 15. Calculating creatinine clearance**

Serum creatinine (in µmol/L)

Serum creatinine (in µmol/L)

In case of creatinine elevation:
* Stop oral PrEP if creatinine elevation is confirmed and if estimated creatinine clearance decreases to <60 ml/min.
* Evaluate for additional causes of creatinine elevations (see Box 12) and manage in consultation with medical officer (MO).
* After oral PrEP is stopped, creatinine should be checked for another one to three months, and oral PrEP can be restarted if CrCl returns to > 60 ml/min.

## **Annex 4: PrEP Counseling and Educational Messages** | **Topic** | **Key Messages** | | --- | --- | | What is PrEP? | ▪ PrEP is the use of antiretroviral drugs by HIV-negative clients to prevent HIV.
▪ It is one of several HIV prevention options and, where possible, should be used in combination with condoms and condom-compatible lubricants and other HIV prevention strategies.
▪ There are four PrEP methods available in Eswatini for PrEP: Tablets taken orally, a ring that is inserted into the vagina and 2 different PrEP injections. Injectable CAB-LA is a PrEP method given as 2-monthly injections while LEN is a 6-monthly injection. |

heading_path: 6 Annexes > Annex 4: PrEP Counseling and Educational Messages
text:
| **Topic** | **Key Messages** | | --- | --- | | Effectiveness of PrEP | ▪ When used as prescribed, oral PrEP is more than 90% effective at preventing HIV acquisition and the PrEP ring is about 50% effective (likely more with effective use). CAB-LA and LEN are most effective in preventing HIV, more than 90% compared to oral PrEP. This is likely due to improved adherence with injections.
▪ When choosing a PrEP method, it is important to consider which method(s) will work best for you to prevent HIV during the types of exposures you anticipate, among other factors.

**For people assigned female at birth (AFAB) interested in PrEP:**
▪ Daily oral PrEP, CAB-LA and LEN reduce your chance of getting HIV during all types of exposures to HIV.
▪ The PrEP ring works only for sexual exposures during receptive vaginal sex.

**For people assigned male at birth (AMAB) interested in PrEP:**
▪ Daily oral PrEP, CAB-LA and LEN reduces your chances of getting HIV during all types of exposures to HIV
▪ Event-drive PrEP, known as ED-PrEP, works only for sexual exposures and can only be used if you are not using any estradiol-based hormones. | | PrEP is not for life | ▪ You should take PrEP for as long as you feel you may be exposed to HIV.
▪ Some people need to take PrEP only during certain times in their lives, while others have an ongoing need to use PrEP.
▪ If you decide to start oral PrEP or the PrEP ring, you should come back every three months for a follow-up visit,. |

text:
| **Topic** | **Key Messages** | | --- | --- | | PrEP and other medications | **Oral PrEP**
▪ Oral PrEP can be taken with hormonal contraceptives and other medications.
▪ For people AMAB using estradiol-based exogenous hormones, there is some indication that the use of estradiol-based hormones may reduce oral PrEP drug levels; therefore, ED-PrEP is not recommended for this population.
▪ Oral PrEP use does not seem to affect levels of estradiol-based exogenous hormones when they are used together.

**The PrEP ring**
▪ The ring can be used with most hormonal contraceptives and barrier methods, including condoms and condom-compatible lubricant.
▪ Using the ring with a diaphragm or another vaginal ring, such as a contraceptive vaginal ring, is not recommended.
▪ There are no known interactions between dapivirine, and the hormones used for gender-affirming hormone therapy.

**Injectable PrEP**
▪ Injectable PrEP, both CAB-LA and LEN can be taken with hormonal contraceptives, gender-affirming hormones, and most other medication.
▪ Some medicines are not recommended when taking injectable PrEP (CAB-LA or LEN).
▪ It is important to tell your health provider about all other medicines you are taking, particularly when you use medicines to treat or prevent tuberculosis, medicines for | | | seizures/convulsions, high dose of aspirin.
▪ If you take any of these, your provider will discuss whether your PrEP dose needs adjustment, or whether another injectable or a different PrEP option would be safer for you.” |

text:
| **Topic** | **Key Messages** | | --- | --- | | Side effects | \*\*Oral PrEP\*\* ▪ Approximately 10 percent of people using \*\*oral PrEP\*\* may experience side effects. Those who do will typically experience only mild side effects, including: - Gastrointestinal symptoms (diarrhea and nausea, decreased appetite, abdominal cramping, and flatulence) - Dizziness - Headaches ▪ Most of those side effects disappear within one month. However, I can help you manage them. \*\*PrEP ring\*\* ▪ Those who have side effects while using the ring typically experience only mild side effects, including: - Urinary tract infections (UTIs) – experienced by about 15% of users) - Vaginal discharge (experienced by about 7% of users) - Vulvar itching - Pelvic and lower abdominal pain (experienced by about 6% of users) ▪ Contact your provider if you experience any urinary or reproductive tract changes, as these could be a sign of an STI or UTI needing treatment. \*\*Injectable PrEP (CAB-LA and LEN)\*\* ▪ Side effects with CAB-LA or LEN are not common but some people who initiate CAB-LA or LEN may experience: - Headache - Dizziness | | | - Nausea/diarrhea
- Feeling fatigue or feverish
- Localized pain or swelling, redness/bruising at the injection site

▪ Some people may also experience depressive disorders while using CAB-LA, although these are uncommon. If you experience changes in how you are feeling emotionally, let me know so we can discuss how to get you the support you need.

▪ Side effects are more common during the earlier injections and decrease over time. |

text:
### Cabotegravir injectable PrEP (CAB-LA)

CAB-LA is a long-acting PrEP method containing **600 mg of cabotegravir extended-release injectable suspension**. The first two injections are given one month apart, thereafter every two months. CAB-LA has been introduced in Eswatini since 2024.

## **Community initiation and refill**

* Provide PrEP services monthly at the same outreach location to ensure clients can receive their refills.
* Align PrEP refills with other services, e.g., contraceptives refills, refills for non-communicable diseases (NCD), etc.
* For oral PrEP and the vaginal ring, up to three months’ worth of refills can be given at initiation.
* Record initiated client in the PrEP register/Client Management Information System (CMIS).
* Provide each client with an appointment card and indicate the next scheduled visit.
* Ensure the appointment card includes all relevant information (such as PrEP method, refill date, etc.) for the client, who may need to access a health care worker between visits.
* Utilize a PrEP register specific to that provider.
* Report monthly on PrEP use through existing regional reporting structures.
* For ordering, storage, and reconciliation of PrEP commodities, follow routine CMS ordering and standard operating procedures.

heading_path: 3 PrEP Delivery > Acute HIV infection (AHI) assessment > Community peer distribution of the PrEP ring
text:
For the PrEP ring, dispensing can be done by trained community cadres that are already conducting HIVST in the community in the following situations:
* Woman testing HIV negative can be provided the ring to offer some protection until she will come to the facility to start oral or injectable PrEP
* Woman not willing/able to come to a PrEP facility to start another PrEP method.
* Woman preferring the ring over another method or woman already using the ring and due for a refill.

## **Community peer distribution of the PrEP ring**

For the PrEP ring, dispensing can be done by trained community cadres that are already conducting HIVST in the community in the following situations:
* Woman testing HIV negative can be provided the ring to offer some protection until she will come to the facility to start oral or injectable PrEP
* Woman not willing/able to come to a PrEP facility to start another PrEP method.
* Woman preferring the ring over another method or woman already using the ring and due for a refill.

text:
## **2.2 Essential package of ANC interventions**

Although the country has never had comprehensive ANC guidelines, there has been a set of interventions on good clinical practice that continue to be implemented as part of the essential ANC package of interventions. These interventions shall be maintained and aligned to the recommended schedule of ANC contacts. The essential package of ANC interventions will be as follows:
| **Contact** | **Maternal Assessment** | **Foetal Assessment** | **Counseling Topics ( Information, education and counseling)** | **Point of Care Tests** | **Lab Investigations** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Contact 1 at 8- 12 weeks** | Comprehensive history taking,, clinical estimation of gestational age; Examination head to toe; ,TB screening, screening for IPV |  | Nutrition; diet; physical activity, rest, HIV test and partner testing, adherence to medicines prescribed,; danger signs, emergency preparedness, early stimulation of the baby, VMMC Counselling, condom usage, avoid: caffeine intake, alcohol/ tobacco/ substance abuse | HIV, Syphilis, Hep B, urine dipstick, Malaria, Hb | Blood group and Rhesus; full blood count, check for ASB (Gram stain or Culture), viral load, CD4 count ,Hep B, |

heading_path: 3.6 Preventive measures > If a pregnant woman received
text:
Diagram: Infographic showing Td vaccination recommendations based on prior TTCV doses (section: *If a pregnant woman received:*)
- No TTCV doses or has unknown vaccination status -> (*she will need*) a) 1 Td dose as early as possible b) 1 Td dose at least 4 weeks later c) 1 Td dose at least 6 months later d) 1 Td dose at least 1 year later e) 1 more Td dose at least 1 year later (to obtain long-term protection)
- Only 3TTCV doses in childhood -> (*she will need*) a) 1 Td dose at the first ANC visit b) Another Td dose 4 weeks later (to be protected for that pregnancy) c) 1 more Td dose at least 1 year later (to obtain long-term protection)
- 4 TTCV doses in childhood -> (*she will need*) a) 1Td dose at that visit (to be protected for that pregnancy) b) 1 more Td dose at least 1 year later (to obtain long-term protection)
- 3 TTCV doses in childhood and 1Td or 1 DT dose later -> (*she will need*) a) 1 TD dose at that visit (to be protected for that pregnancy) b) 1 more Td dose at least 1 year later (to obtain long-term protection)
- 4 TTCV doses in childhood and 1 Td dose later -> (*she will need*) 1 TD dose at that contact (no further doses required)
- 4 TTCV doses and 2 Td boosters -> (*she will need*) No vaccination, the woman is fully protected

Opened cervix

Uterus smaller than dates

text:
## *6.3.3 Diagnosis of Antepartum haemorrhage* | **Probable diagnosis** | **Signs and symptoms** | **Management** | | --- | --- | --- | | **Abruptio placenta** | • Vaginal Bleeding
• Intermittent or constant abdominal pain
• Shock
• Tender tense uterus
• Decreased or absent fetal movement
• Fetal distress or absent fetal sounds | General management
***Shout for help!!!! (Inyandzaleyo!!!!)***
• Follow A, B, C:
o Airways clear
o Breathing
o Circulation
• Assess the hemodynamics status of the patient.
• Vital signs: pulse, blood pressure and do urgent ward HB.
• **NOTE:** Tachycardia should be taken seriously even in a stable looking patient, confusion and restlessness.
• Resuscitate the patient as appropriate
o Insert 2 large IV lines.
o Correct hypovolaemia using normal saline or Ringer’s Lactate
o Strict fluid balance chart. Insert Foleys catheter. Monitor input and output.
o If available give oxygen 4 to 6 L per minute to the mother by facemask.
o Blood grouping and cross match, FBC.
**Refer the patient to hospital as soon as possible.**
**NOTE: DO NOT PERFORM DIGITAL VAGINAL EXAMINATION UNTIL PLACENTA PRAEVIA IS RULED OUT.** | | **Placenta praevia** | • Vaginal bleeding (painless and bright red in colour) may be precipitated by intercourse
• Shock
• Relaxed uterus
• Fetal presentation not in the pelvis; malpresentation, lower uterine pole feels empty
Normal fetal condition | |

### *6.5.2 Risk Factors and symptoms*

| **Risk factors:** | **Symptoms:** | **Management** |

| • 1st pregnancy | • May be asymptomatic | • Urgently refer the patient to the nearest hospital |
| • Age >40yrs | • Headache not relieved by simple analgesia | • Give pre -referral loading dose of Mg Sulphate 4g IM |
| • Overweight (BMI >35 at 1st ANC visit) | • Altered mental state | • For patient with convulsion: |
| • Family history of PIH/ pre - eclampsia | • Blindness | • Do not leave the patient alone. |
| • Multiple pregnancy | • Shortness of breath | • Shout for assistance. State “Eclampsia” |
| • Last pregnancy was> 10 years ago | • Blurred vision or flashing | • Turn patient to left lateral position. |
| • Chronic kidney dis ease | • Epigastric pain /Right upper quadrant abdominal pain | • Ensure that the airway is clear and the patient breathing. |
| • Diabetes Mellitus | • Rapid swelling of face, hands and feet | • Protect the patient from falling, injury. |
| • Autoimmune diseases | • Nonspecific complaints of being unwell | • Do not place anything in the mouth. |
| • Race -black | • Convulsions | • Oxygen by mask at 4-6 L per minute. |
| • Chronic hypertension |  | • When convulsion ends, start IV. |

#### ***6.6.1 Definition***

* Premature rupture of membranes (PROM) is the drainage of amniotic fluid through the cervical canal before the onset of uterine contractions.
* **PROM** may be **Pre-term (before 37 weeks of gestation)** or **at-Term (post 37 weeks of gestation)**.

text: Quality ANC is provided in a continuum linking the individual, family and community with the health facility. Support from community and facility based health care providers can enhance the care provided to pregnant women.

heading_path: Key Definitions
text:
## **Key Definitions**

| Term | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| Adolescents | Refers to people aged 10-19 years. |
| Associate | This refers to an approach led by HIV positive peer workers, who are trained to create and manage a “referral chain network”. Peer mobilizers have undergone HIV testing (and, if HIV positive, are enrolled in treatment); they pass referral slips for HIV testing to members of their social, sexual or drug networks. |
| Bidirectional referral | System considers both the information going from the health care system to the referred community program or resource |
| Children | Refers to people aged 0-9 years. |
| Community referral | This is a referral of a client made at community level by a Community Health care worker (Rural Health Motivators/ Community Expert Client/Community Mentor Mother) to the nearest health facility (clinic, health center, hospital). |
| Facility referral | This is a referral of a client made at health facility level by facility and health care workers within the same health facility (Intra-facility) or to another health facility (inter facility) for care that the health care workers do not have the capacity to provide. |
| Intra Facility | This is a referral made within different departments in the same health facility. |
| Inter facility | This is a referral made from one health facility to another health facility. |
| HIV index case | This is an individual diagnosed with HIV infection who draws attention to his/her sexual partner(s)/injecting drug users, biological children below 15 years and associates for HIV testing services. |

heading_path: Key Definitions
text:
| Term | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| HIV Self-testing | This is a process where an individual collects his or her specimen, performs a test and the results, often in a private setting, either alone or with someone he or she trusts. |
| Index contact | These are people who have had contact with the index case in a way which is associated with HIV transmission. It includes biological child(ren) <15 with an unknown status, partners, and associates. |
| Index case testing | This refers to an approach focused on testing individuals in the social or sexual networks of index cases, including children below the age of 15 years, sexual partners, needle-sharing partners, and other high-risk contacts. Index case testing describes the process of tracing and offering HIV testing services to the children, and partner(s) of both newly identified HIV infected individuals and those of already known HIV positive status; with a goal to identify those infected with HIV but are not aware of their infection or those with known HIV positive status not currently in HIV care. |
| Linkage to Care and Treatment | This is a process in which the client has reached the facility and provided with care and treatment services he/she needs. The referring facility verifies if the client has arrived and was provided with services, or the receiving facility gives feedback to the referring facility. |
| Linkage case management | Linkage case management (LCM) comprises the package of linkage services including individualized case management; treatment navigation and index testing. |

heading_path: 5 Linkage to Treatment and Care > 5.4 Summary of Linkage case management services > Guiding Principles for Linkage Case Management
text:
# <mark>Guiding Principles for Linkage Case Management</mark>

| 1. | LCM is voluntary; all eligible patients are free to enroll or discontinue services. |
| --- | --- |
| 2. | Quality and Inclusiveness; LCM should ensure that partners, family members, and associates of LCM clients are appropriately HIV diagnosed and linked to ART care. |
| 3. | Client centered: LCM should focus on the patient's client's concerns and priorities or must focus on problem solving approach to address concerns |
| 4. | Teamwork: Providers of LCM including clinicians, peers, lay staff, community workers, families, and the clients themselves should strive to always work together. |
| 5. | Transparency: Providers of LCM should ensure good communication at all stages of LCM implementation. |

| **Goal** | Reduce TB incidence by 40% relative to the 2022 levels / Reduce TB deaths by 50% by 2028 relative to the 2022 levels. / Eliminate catastrophic costs (0%) for recipients of care and their household members. |
| **Strategic Objectives** | - To achieve 90% TB treatment coverage by 2028. - To strengthen primary and secondary TB prevention services. - To achieve a 90% treatment success rate for all forms of TB including DS-TB and DR-TB. - To improve TB screening, diagnosis, treatment and prevention among children and adolescents. - To improve the quality and utilization of TB Information for decision-making and programmatic actions. - To strengthen governance structures and organizational capacity for optimal program management. |

## BREATH IN AND OUT 3 TIMES

| Step | Action |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Breathe in deeply |
| 2 | Hold the air for 5 seconds |
| 3 | Breathe out slowly |
| 4 | Repeat steps 1-3 three times |
| 5 | Cough out hard from the chest |
| 6 | Spit sputum into plastic bottle |

text:
Upon receiving the Xpert results, treatment decisions should be made as follows:
| MTB was Detected and Rifampicin resistance not detected |  |
| --- | --- |
| (All patients whose diagnosis of TB has been confirmed by Xpert® MTB/RIF Ultra but without evidence of Rifampicin resistance) |  |
| *Should be registered as MTBC positive, bacteriologically confirmed TB = MTB+ve/Rif-ve* |  |
| *Reflex Xpert MTB/XDR Assay should be done to rule out INH and fluoroquinolone resistance.* |  |
| *Facilities with Xpert MTB/XDR onsite are to initiate treatment after receiving Xpert MTB/XDR assay results.* |  |
| *Start first-line anti-TB treatment for MTB +ve/Rif -ve while waiting for Xpert MTB/XDR and DST results if not available onsite* |  |
| *All Xpert positive (MTB +ve/Rif-ve) cases must have reflex MGIT culture and DST done on a second sample at the time of diagnosis* |  |
| *Xpert MTB-positive patients should be monitored while on treatment using smear microscopy at the recommended intervals until completion of treatment.* |  |
| **Note:** *Xpert MTB/RIF® Ultra can detect dead bacilli so culture confirmation is needed for previously treated cases. Awaiting culture, should not delay initiation of TB treatment but treatment should be based on the clinical condition of the patient. If in doubt, it is also important to consult a Medical Officer.* |  |

text:
Diagram: Algorithm to evaluate for TB among PLHIV (section: Figure 18: Algorithm to evaluate for TB among PLHIV)
- • Assess for TB signs and symptoms (S/S)†; • Assess if seriously ill*; • Assess for advanced HIV disease (AHD); • Perform CD4 testing (if eligible); • Perform CXR/CRP screening if eligible (if available) † -> Positive for TB S/S and/or CXR/CRP positive for possible TB regardless of CD4 count /AHD status; AHD regardless of TB S/S or seriously ill; No TB S/S, CXR/CRP Negative for possible TB CD4 >200 or unknown
- Positive for TB S/S and/or CXR/CRP positive for possible TB regardless of CD4 count /AHD status -> Perform Xpert MTB/Rif (Ultra) and Urine LAM tests (if not yet performed)
- AHD regardless of TB S/S or seriously ill -> Perform Urine LAM
- Perform Urine LAM -> LAM positive; LAM negative
- LAM positive -> Perform Xpert MTB/Rif (Ultra) and Urine LAM tests (if not yet performed)
- Perform Xpert MTB/Rif (Ultra) and Urine LAM tests (if not yet performed) -> Both Xpert and LAM negative; Xpert AND/OR LAM positive
- Both Xpert and LAM negative -> • Clinical management; • Provide TPT if eligible
- Xpert AND/OR LAM positive -> • Start TB treatment; • Perform work-up to exclude DR-TB (collect specimen for phenotypic and genotypic DST of anti-TB drugs
- LAM negative -> Apply AHD package of care
- No TB S/S, CXR/CRP Negative for possible TB CD4 >200 or unknown -> • Clinical management; • Provide TPT if eligible

Positive TB signs and symptoms and/or CXR/CRP positive, regardless of CD4 or AHD status: do Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra and urine LAM. Xpert and/or LAM positive: start TB treatment and work up to exclude DR-TB (phenotypic and genotypic DST). Both negative: clinical management and TPT if eligible. AHD regardless of TB signs and symptoms, or seriously ill: do urine LAM. LAM positive: do Xpert and LAM tests as above. LAM negative: apply the AHD package of care. No TB signs and symptoms, CXR/CRP negative, CD4 above 200 or unknown: clinical management and TPT if eligible.

heading_path: 5.3 Disposal of Laboratory Materials
text:
## 5.3 Disposal of Laboratory Materials

TB Specimens examined in the laboratory are potentially infectious. Hence, after examination, they must be disinfected and destroyed so that the risk of infection is reduced. All disposable containers must be used only once. Sputum cups which contain sputum can be disposed of by any one of the following methods:
|  | Description |
| --- | --- |
| **Disinfection** | After the TB specimens have been used, all sputum cups should be kept in a bucket containing 5% hypochlorite, 10% bleach solution (freshly prepared), or 5% phenol solution. The caps of the sputum cups must be removed and the cups, caps and wooden sticks completely submerged in the solution in a secure place for at least 18 hours. After this, the solution, cups, caps and wooden sticks can be discarded with other hospital waste. This bin/bucket should have a lid which is foot operated. |
| **Incineration** | Wherever incinerators exist, the type specified under the Biomedical Waste Management & Handling Rules of the country, with a combustion efficiency of 99%, should be used. Sputum cups made of polypropylene should be used wherever available. (Note: If sputum cups are made of other varieties of plastic, they should be disinfected and destroyed as per the hospital waste management rules). *Burning is NOT recommended*. |

heading_path: Chapter 8: Childhood TB Screening, Diagnosis and Treatment > 8.3 Diagnosis of Childhood TB > Table 32: Procedures of respiratory sample and stool sample collection
text:
| Method | Techniques | | --- | --- | | **Sputum Induction** | | | **Gastric Aspirate** | • Consider in children < 7 years
• Nasogastric aspiration of gastric secretions using a nasogastric tube
• 2-3 specimens are recommended to increase yield
• Volume: 5-10 ml should be collected, if less confirm tube placement and re-attempt. If still < 5-10 ml instill up to 20 ml of sterile water and re-aspirate.
• It should be performed in the early morning and fast for 4 hours (outpatient collection is fine provided these parameters are met).
• Nasogastric tube should be used
• If possible, neutralize the aspirate with sodium bicarbonate if the specimen is not processed that day based on pH testing | | **Nasopharyngeal Aspirate** | • Can be performed in children under 6 years
• Suctioning of the nasopharynx via a nasopharyngeal tube at 15 -20 kPa of pressure
• 2 ml of aspirate is recommended
• Can be performed at any time but morning is preferred, generally follows sputum induction
• A suction machine is recommended for the procedure |

doc_title: National Integrated Tuberculosis Management Guidelines (2025)
heading_path: Chapter 8: Childhood TB Screening, Diagnosis and Treatment > 8.3 Diagnosis of Childhood TB > Table 32: Procedures of respiratory sample and stool sample collection
text:
| Method | Techniques | | --- | --- | | **Stool for TB** | • Performed only for children under the age of 15 years.
• For infants and toddlers, stools can be directly collected from the diaper as soon as possible after defecation. \*(Avoiding prolonged contact with the surface of the diaper.)\*
• Older children are directed to defecate on a clean sheet of paper, avoiding contamination from the soil and urine.
• Using a designated spatula or wooden stick, the sample is transferred into a stool container or a sputum container and sealed tightly before submitting it to the laboratory for processing. The sample container should NOT be filled to the brim.
• A volume of 1g (a pea size) for a formed stool or 5 ml for a watery stool is sufficient to perform the Xpert test.
• The simple one-step method (SOS) is used in the laboratory to analyse the sample.
• A subsequently induced sputum or gastric aspirate will have to be collected and sent for culture and DST to the reference lab should the Xpert MTB results turn out positive. | | **Methods of specimen collection for Extra-Pulmonary Disease** | • Specimen collection should be attempted from the presumed site of disease through fine needle aspiration of lymph nodes, collection of CSFS, pleural, ascetic fluid etc. |

narrative: TB screening algorithm for children under 15 years attending a health facility (TB guidelines 2025, figure 23, page 156). Symptom screen: current cough, fever, weight loss or night sweats for ages 10-15; cough, fever, weight loss or poor weight gain of any duration, or TB contact history for under 10. If positive, collect two specimens (one stool sample if under 5 or unable to produce sputum) for microbiological assessment, including LF-LAM for children living with HIV. Positive: initiate TB treatment. Negative: clinical assessment of active TB if symptoms persist or other morbidity, take a CXR if not taken before, and provide TB preventive therapy (TPT) if eligible. If symptom screen is negative, assess risk factors (child TB contacts, nutrition status with MUAC below 12.5 cm under 5 years or below 22.5 cm over 5 years, vulnerable children such as orphans). No risk factors: exit. Risk factors: check whether CXR was done in the past 12 months; if yes, further clinical evaluation and TPT if eligible; if no, CXR read by a human reader; negative, TPT evaluation; non-TB abnormality, clinical assessment and TPT if eligible. Perform TB-LAM for all advanced HIV disease (CD4 below 200 or WHO stage 3-4), seriously ill children, and all presumptive TB.

If CXR was taken in the past 12 months, evaluate and provide TPT if eligible; if not, CXR screen by a human reader (negative, evaluate and give TPT; positive, microbiological assessment).

text:
## **Table 39: Guide to management of side effects of first line**

| Side effects | Drugs (probably responsible) | Management |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Major |  |  |
| Generalized severe skin rash with or without itching | Isoniazid, Rifampicin, Pyrazinamide and Ethambutol | Stop anti-TB drugs and refer. Re-challenge once stable, starting with the least likely causative agent. Give antihistamines to manage pruritis |
| Deafness (no wax on otoscopy) | Injectable \* | Stop Injectable and refer |
| Dizziness (vertigo and nystagmus) | Injectable \* | Stop Injectable and refer |
| Jaundice (other causes excluded), hepatitis | Pyrazinamide, INH, Rifampicin | Stop anti-TB drugs and refer Re-challenge once stable starting with the least hepatotoxic agent |
| Confusion (suspect drug-induced acute liver failure if there is jaundice) | Most anti-TB drugs | Stop anti-TB drugs and refer |
| Visual impairment (other causes excluded) | Ethambutol | Stop Ethambutol and refer |
| Shock, purpura, acute renal failure | Rifampicin | Stop Rifampicin and refer |
| Decreased urine output (acute renal failure) | Injectable \* | Stop Injectable and refer Adjust the doses of other renally-excreted drugs e.g. Ethambutol |
| Minor |  |  |

narrative: Management of QTc prolongation from second-line TB drugs (TB guidelines 2025, figure 28, page 186). Causative drugs: bedaquiline (BDQ), clofazimine (CFZ), moxifloxacin (MFX), delamanid (DLM), levofloxacin (LFX). Monitor with an ECG at baseline, week 2 and monthly until month 6, or any time with symptoms (palpitations, fainting, dizziness). If QTcF is prolonged, repeat the ECG and consider other causes (low potassium, malnutrition, hypothyroidism, other drugs); check and replace potassium if vomiting or diarrhoea. Grade 1 (QTcF printed as "45 - 480 msec", presumably 450-480) and grade 2 (above 480-500 msec): monitor closely with weekly ECG until QTcF is below the grade or at baseline, and correct electrolytes or other causes. Grade 3 (above 500 msec): stop the suspected drug(s), hospitalise and correct electrolytes or causes. Grade 4 (above 501 msec or 60 msec change from baseline plus torsades de pointes, polymorphic ventricular tachycardia or serious arrhythmia): stop the suspected drugs, hospitalise and correct causes. If on multiple QTcF-prolonging drugs, stop ancillary drugs first, then MFX, then if prolongation persists CFZ, then BDQ.

Causative drugs: pyrazinamide (PZA), isoniazid (INH), bedaquiline (BDQ), clofazimine (CFZ), ethionamide (Eto), PAS. Monitor liver function tests at baseline and monthly for the first six months, and any time with symptoms (abdominal pain, nausea or vomiting, jaundice, itching). Assess other causes (alcohol, traditional medicines or herbs, viral hepatitis, TB itself). Grade 1 (above 1 to 2.5 times the upper limit of normal, ULN, asymptomatic) and grade 2 (above 2.5 to 5 times ULN, asymptomatic): continue treatment and follow until AST/ALT returns to baseline or stabilises. Grade 3 (above 5 to 10 times ULN, or any symptomatic elevation) and grade 4 (above 10 times ULN regardless of symptoms): stop all drugs, measure LFTs weekly, and reintroduce drugs after toxicity resolves.

heading_path: 10.1 TB/HIV interaction and the comprehensive package of care > 10.1.5 When to start ART? > Table 45: Recommended periods to start ART in PLHIV with presumptive TB and confirmed TB
text:
### **Table 45: Recommended periods to start ART in PLHIV with presumptive TB and confirmed TB**

| **Patient Category** | **When to start ART** |
| --- | --- |
| **Among PLHIV who are presumptive for TB** | Initiate ART while rapidly investigating for TB, with close follow-up within seven days to initiate TB treatment if TB is confirmed |
| **Among PLHIV on ART and diagnosed with TB** | Continue ART and initiate anti-TB treatment as soon as diagnosed, may need to adjust ART regimen/dosage if required |
| **For newly diagnosed PLHIV/returnees who also have been diagnosed with TB** | Initiate ART as soon as possible preferably within 2 weeks of initiating tuberculosis treatment (including same-day anti-TB and ART treatment if clinically stable) regardless of immune status |
| **Patients with TB meningitis** | Delay ART to 4 weeks post-initiation of anti-TB treatment |

heading_path: 10.1 TB/HIV interaction and the comprehensive package of care > Table 47: TB treatment/ART Drug Interactions
text:
# Table 47: TB treatment/ART Drug Interactions

| Drug combination | Considerations |
| --- | --- |
| Rifampicin and (LPV/r) | - LPV/r can be used with Rifampicin - Super boost the LPV/r (1:1 lopinavir and ritonavir) by adding ritonavir. - Closely monitor the client for toxicity (especially gastrointestinal intolerance) and virological failure |
| Rifampicin and Oral Contraceptive Pill | - Oral contraceptive pills may not be effective when administered with RIF. - Women of childbearing age should either receive a contraceptive pill containing a higher dose of oestrogen (50μg) or use another form of contraception (e.g., medroxyprogesterone). - Emphasize concomitant condom use during this period |
| DTG and all TB treatments | - Preference is for clients to be maintained on a fixed dose combination of TDF+3TC+EFV for the duration of TB treatment. - Check VL at the end of TB treatment. If the VL is undetectable: the client can be transitioned to a once-daily FDC of TDF+3TC+DTG two weeks after completion of TB treatment. If the VL is detectable, immediately switch to the second line and continue adherence support. - If the client is on a DTG regimen, the DTG does need to be given as 50mg twice daily until at least 2 weeks after the client has completed TB treatment. This may increase the occurrence of DTG side effects. |

text:
Diagram: Algorithm for ruling out active TB/DR-TB disease in HIV negative household contacts >10 years old and other risk groups (section: Neither CXR nor TBI test is mandatory to make a decision to start TPT)
- Household TB contacts. Other Risk Groups* -> Symptom based screening (CXR if available)
- Symptom based screening (CXR if available) -> Positive (S/S and/or CXC); *Negative (S/S and/or CXC)
- Positive (S/S and/or CXC) -> Evaluate for TB/DR-TB
- Evaluate for TB/DR-TB -> TB/DR-TB disease; No TB
- TB/DR-TB disease -> Treat for TB/DR-TB
- No TB -> Start TPT
- *Negative (S/S and/or CXC) -> Perform TBI Test; TBI test unavailable and household contact
- Perform TBI Test -> Positive; Negative; Indeterminate
- Positive -> Start TPT
- Negative -> No TPT
- Indeterminate -> No TPT
- TBI test unavailable and household contact -> Start TPT

heading_path: 11.13 TPT completion and management of TBI treatment interruption > Table 62: Management of TPT interruption or missed dose
text:
### **Table 62: Management of TPT interruption or missed dose**

| **TPT regimen** | **Duration of treatment interruption** | **Next Steps** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **3HP** | 1 weekly dose missed | If the missed dose is remembered within the next 2 days, continue to take the remaining doses according to the original schedule. If the missed dose is remembered > 2 days later, take the missed dose immediately, and change the schedule for weekly intake to the day the missed dose was taken, until treatment completion. This will avoid 2 weekly doses being taken fewer than 4 days apart. |
|  | More than 1 weekly doses missed | If treatment interruption occurred after at least 9 doses were taken within 12 weeks of starting, continue and complete the remaining doses, thus prolonging the total treatment duration to a maximum of 112 days. If ≥ 4 weekly doses are missed, consider restarting the full TPT course. If an individual has difficulty adhering to a weekly routine, consider dis continuing 3HP and offering an alternative regimen with daily dosing. |
| **1HP** | Less than 7 doses missed | Continue and complete the remaining doses, thus prolonging the total treatment duration to a maximum of 6 weeks (42 days from starting TPT) |

| --- | --- |
| • Encourages partner’s communication on contraception | • Both partners must decide, agree and be fully committed to use abstinence. |

| • Delays sexual debut for the adolescents and young people |  |
| • Provides 100% protection against pregnancy and reduces risk of sexually transmitted infections and HIV. |  |

heading_path: 5 Natural Family Planning Method > 5.3 Fertility Awareness Methods > Advantages and disadvantages
text:
## **Advantages and disadvantages**

| Advantages | Disadvantages |
| --- | --- |
| • Fertility Awareness methods have no side effects. | • No protection against sexually transmitted infections including HIV |
| • Improve knowledge of the reproductive system and understanding of menstrual cycle. | • Need cooperation and commitment by both partners. |
| • Shared responsibility by partners. | • Require intensive education and instruction before being confident to use method. |
| • Less expensive. | • May not be easy to use if menstrual cycle is irregular. |
| • Do not require procedures and usually do not require supplies | • Require accurate record keeping. |
| • Limited need for professional consultation. | • Unreliable if client is breastfeeding and has amenorrhea. |
| • Allows some partners to adhere to their religious or cultural norms | • Has a high failure rate if client is not well trained and there is no commitment and cooperation between partners. |
| • Can assist partners in achieving a wanted pregnancy. |  |
| • Return to fertility is immediate. |  |

• No need to wait until the start of next monthly bleeding. | | Amenorrhoea | • Delay until menses return | • Delay until menses return | | After childbirth (whether or not breastfeeding) | • She can start symptoms-based methods once normal vaginal secretions have returned.

## **When a pill or more is missed;**

| **Number of** ***Missed Pills*** | **Action to be taken** |
| --- | --- |
| 1 pill | She should take the pill as soon as she can then continue at the usual time. Use a backup method for 2 days after the missed pill. |
| 2 pills | She should take 2 pills as soon as she can and take another 2 pills the next day then return to her regular schedule on the 3rd day. A backup method of contraception should be used. |
| 3 pills | ***Do not attempt to replace as above;*** She should use a backup method of contraception and report to the health facility for professional help as soon as possible. |

text:
## **Advantages and disadvantages of POPs**

| Advantages | Disadvantages |
| --- | --- |
| • Can be used during breastfeeding anytime between giving birth and 6 months | • Do not protect against STIs including HIV and AIDS |
| • Do not affect breast milk production. | • They require strict daily pill-taking, preferably at the same time each day |
| • Suitable for women with risk factors such as heart attack, stroke and thrombosis. | • Irregular bleeding and spotting is common |
| • Less side effects such as acne and weight gain. | • Less effective in women who are not breastfeeding |
| • Return to fertility is immediate upon discontinuation. | • Effectiveness may decrease if clients are also taking some other medications (anti-TB drugs, anticonvulsants and antiretroviral (Retinovir boosted and NNRTI based, etc) so a client should use a backup method or change the medication/ method altogether. |
| • Non contraceptive health benefits which include prevention of endometrial cancer, and anaemia. | • Effectiveness may also be lowered in the presence of diarrhoea and vomiting |

text:
## **Advantages and disadvantages of POIs**

| Advantages | Disadvantages |
| --- | --- |
| • Can be used during breastfeeding starting after childbirth | • Do not protect against STIs including HIV and AIDS |
| • Do not affect breast milk production | • May cause changes in menstrual bleeding patterns. |
| • Suitable for women with risk factors such as heart attack, stroke and thrombosis. | • May cause indirect weight changes and acne. |
| • Provides highly effective protection against pregnancy. | • Requires repeat injection every 2 or 3 months. |
| • Ensures periodic contact with medical or trained health personnel. | • There may be delayed return to fertility and cannot be reversed immediately. |
| • Only requires to remember the clinic return dates | • May cause headaches, breast tenderness, nausea, hair loss, reduced and changes in libido |
| • It can be confidential: no one else can tell that a woman is using contraception |  |
| • Non-contraceptive health benefits which include prevention of endometrial cancer, uterine fibroids, endometrial cancers, Pelvic Inflammatory Diseases, endometriosis and anaemia. |  |
| • Decreases incidence of pre-menstrual or postmenstrual depression and epileptic seizures |  |
| • Do not make a woman infertile and do not disrupt an existing pregnancy |  |

## **Advantages and disadvantages of using COCs**

| Advantages | Disadvantages |
| --- | --- |
| • Easy to use | • Does not protect against STIs and HIV infection. |
| • Can be used from adolescence to menopause; by nulliparous and multiparous women; provided that no risk factors exist. | • Must be taken daily and at the same time |
| ***Help protect against:*** | • Require an individual to obtain regular supplies. |
| • Risks of pregnancy | • Effectiveness may be lowered if client is on anti-TB drugs (Rifampicin or Rifabutin therapy), anti-epilepsy treatment and some ARVs indicating a need for a backup method. |
| • Cancer of the lining of the uterus (endometrial cancer) | • Effectiveness may also be lowered in the presence of diarrhoea and vomiting |
| • Cancer of the ovary | • Reduce milk production in breastfeeding women. |
| • Symptomatic pelvic inflammatory disease | • May cause mood changes and low libido to some women |
| • Ovarian cysts | • Can increase the risk of Myocardial Infarction (MI) in women with existing risk factors such as smoking, Diabetes or hypertension. |
| • Iron-deficiency anaemia |  |
| • Reduce menstrual cramps |  |
| • Supresses menstrual bleeding problems |  |
| • Reduce ovulation pain |  |
| • Reduce excess hair on face or body |  |
| • Minimises symptoms of polycystic ovarian syndrome (irregular period, acne, excess hair on face or body) |  |
| • Reduce symptoms of endometriosis (pelvic pain, irregular bleeding) |  |

heading_path: 7 Intrauterine Contraception Device > Advantages and disadvantages
text:
## **Advantages and disadvantages**

| Advantages | Disadvantages |
| --- | --- |
| • Reliable long term contraceptive method (protection up-to 10 years) | • Does not protect against STIs including HIV |
| • Safe to use during breastfeeding | • May increase menstrual bleeding and cramping in the first few months of use |
| • Does not interfere with sexual intercourse | *Though *Uncommon:** |
| • Has no further costs for supplies after the IUCD is inserted | • May contribute to anemia if a woman already has low iron blood stores before insertion |
| • Does not require client action for efficacy | • May cause Pelvic Inflammatory Disease in woman with chlamydia or gonorrhoea at the time of IUCD insertion. |
| • May help protect against cancer of the lining of the uterus (endometrial cancer) |  |
| • May help protect against cervical cancer |  |
| • Reduces the risk of ectopic pregnancy |  |
| • No hormonal side effects with Copper T |  |
| • Hormone releasing IUCD may reduce menstrual bleeding and immediate return to fertility |  |

text:
## **Advantages and disadvantages**

| Advantages | Disadvantages |
| --- | --- |
| • Reduces the risk of pregnancy | • No protection against STIs including HIV |
| • Can be used by women of any age, including adolescents | • Failure rate of ECPs is higher as compared to other contraceptives |
| • They are not abortifacient | • Does not provide long term protection |
| • Do not prevent or affect implantation | • EC pills do not continue to prevent pregnancy during the rest of the cycle. |
| • Do not cause birth defects if pregnancy occurs | • EC has the potential for misuse through self-prescription and sharing of pills. |
| • Are not dangerous to a woman’s health | • Efficacy depends on the client action. |
| • Do not increase risky sexual behaviour | • They can cause nausea (more common for the COC regimen) |
| • Do not make women infertile |  |
| • Can be used more than once in a woman’s cycle |  |

heading_path: 9 Surgical Sterilization > Advantages and disadvantages
text:
## **Advantages and disadvantages**

| Advantages | Disadvantages |
| --- | --- |
| • Protects against pregnancy | • Does not protect against STIs and HIV. |
| • Is highly effective and safe | • Difficult to reverse. |
| • Efficacy does not depend on the client’s action. | • Procedure needs specially equipped facilities and trained personnel. |
| • Has no effects on breastfeeding | • Failure of procedure pre-disposes to ectopic pregnancy. |
| • Does not interfere with act of sexual intercourse. | • Subjects client to pain and leaves permanent scar. |
| • It is cost effective after the initial procedure | • The client /partner needs to sign a consent |
| • No significant long term side effects or health risks. | • There may be complications associated with the surgical procedure such as infection and or bleeding at incision site |
| • It protects against ovarian cancer |  |
| • It is effective immediately after the procedure |  |
| • Reduces the risk of ectopic pregnancy. |  |

heading_path: 10 Barrier Methods > Advantages and disadvantages
text:
## **Advantages and disadvantages**

| Advantages | Disadvantages |
| --- | --- |
| • Prevent most STIs, including HIV/AIDS when used correctly and consistently with every act of sexual intercourse. | • Efficacy depends on the client’s knowledge on condom use and mutual agreement of partners. |
| • They prevent pregnancy. | • Availability has to be ensured by carrying it at all times. |
| • Encourages involvement of both partners during sexual intercourse. | • Could slip in or off during sex. |
| • Can be used with other contraceptive methods (dual method use). | • Quality is compromised with poor storage. |
| • Have no hormonal side effects and may reduce exposure to cervical cancer. | • Not re-usable. |
| • Have no effect on breast milk production. | • It interrupts the sexual activity. |
| • Relatively easy to use | • Spillage or condom burst. |
| • They are relatively inexpensive and widely accessible. |  |
| • Do not require medical consultation or contact with health care providers. |  |
| • Empowers women to protect themselves from pregnancy, STIs including HIV. |  |
| • No medical conditions appear to limit use. |  |
| • Promotes good hygiene habbits. |  |
| • It does not interfere with fertility. |  |

text:
### **11.1 Why integrate FP services?**

| Importance of integration | Challenges of integration |
| --- | --- |
| • Clients benefit from multiple services in one visit | • Client load can make it difficult to offer comprehensive FP services in some areas |
| • Missed opportunities for some services are minimized | • Staff attitude. |
| • There is increased uptake of services | • Increased waiting time for clients (some may be in a hurry) |
| • Minimizes referrals | • Shortage of human resources. |
| • Integration improves the engagement of both sexes |  |

Women living with severe or advanced HIV clinical disease (WHO stage 3 or 4)** | Women living with severe or advanced HIV clinical disease (WHO stage 3 or 4) can use the following *hormonal* contraceptive methods without restriction: *COCs,* CICs, combined contraceptive patches and *rings,* POPs, POIs (DMPA and NET-EN), and LNG and ETG implants (MEC Category 1).

Women living with severe or advanced HIV clinical disease (WHO stage 3 or 4) generally should not initiate use of the LNG-IUD (MEC Category 3) until their illness has improved *to asymptomatic* or mild HIV clinical disease (WHO stage 1 or 2).

Women who already have an LNG-IUD inserted and who develop severe or advanced HIV clinical disease *need* not have their IUD removed (MEC Category 2 for *continuation).* | |

For the 16 women who became pregnant in this study, the mean time elapsed between implant insertion and pregnancy was 16.4 months.

Several case reports and a pharmacokinetic study suggest that efavirenz (but not ritonavir -boosted lopinavir) may decrease the efficacy of Etonogestrel implants (e.g., Implanon), though additional data are needed. In a Brazilian study, 79 women living with HIV received Etonogestrel implants and were followed every 6 months for 3 years. Over the course of the study, between 60 percent and 71 percent of women were receiving various ART regimens; no pregnancies were reported. | | Levonorgestrel releasing intrauterine devices (IUDs) (e.g., Mirena) | Limited evidence suggests that efficacy of the Levonorgestrel releasing IUD is unlikely to be affected by ART. | | Emergency contraceptive pills (ECPs) | Limited evidence suggests that Levonorgestrel levels are significantly reduced among women using LNG ECPs and efavirenz, but no efficacy data are available. doc_title: WHO Mental Health Deskguide (2022)
heading_path: Definition of Terms
text:
## **DEFINITION OF TERMS**

| **Affect** - observable emotional response seen in the person’s non-verbal behavior. |
| --- |
| **Delusions** - Irrational, strong beliefs which have no basis in reality but which cannot be changed by logic or argument. |
| **Disability** – refers to any impairment which may be physical, mental, and developmental or a combination of these. |
| **Fear** - The body’s physiologic and emotional response to a known or recognized danger. |
| **Flight of ideas** – is a symptom that is common in BAD mania patients manifested by expressing many ideas at the same time (jumping from topic to topic). |
| **Grandiose delusions** – abnormal fixed beliefs of expansive ideas such as inflated worth, power, knowledge, identity or special relationship to a famous person. |
| **Hallucinations** - perceptions that occur in the absence of any appropriate external stimuli and could be of any of the five senses. |
| **Illusion** - a false interpretation or perception of a real environmental stimulus that may involve any of the five senses. |
| **Insomnia** – inability to sleep well either difficulty in initiating and/or maintaining sleep or interrupted sleeping pattern. |
| **Impulsivity** - behavior characterized by little or no forethought, reflection, or consideration of the consequences. |
| **Mental Status Examination (MSE)** - a structured way of observing and describing a patient’s current state of mind under the domains of appearance, attitude, behavior, mood, speech, thought process, thought content, perception, cognitions, judgment and insight |

text:
## TABLE 5: SUMMARY OF CLASSIFICATION AND MANAGEMENT OF TRAUMA AND STRESSOR RELATED DISORDERS | SIGNS | CLASSIFIED AS: | MANAGEMENT | | --- | --- | --- | | The following are diagnostic criteria;
\*\*A.\*\* If the patient was exposed to actual or threatened death, serious injury or sexual violence in one or more of the following ways;
- Directly experienced the trauma
- Witnessed the event(s) as it occurred to others
- Learned the event(s) occurred to a close relative or friend
- Experienced repeated or extreme exposure to a traumatic event(s) (does not apply to exposure through electronic media, TV, movies, pictures unless the exposure is work related)
Duration of symptoms (criteria B,C, D and E) is more than one month.
\*\*B.\*\* Presence of one or more of the following symptoms:
- Recurrent involuntary and intrusive distressing memories of traumatic event(s). (in children repetitive play may occur in which themes or aspects of the traumatic event(s) are expressed.
- Recurrent distressing dreams of the traumatic event(s). In children there may be frightening dreams.
- Flash backs of the event(s)
- Intense or prolonged psychological distress at exposure to cues that symbolizes or resembles the traumatic event(s) | POST TRAUMATIC STRESS DISORDER (PTSD) | - Assess and provide counseling
- Refer to the Clinical Psychologist for psychotherapy if there is no improvement with counseling
- Prescribe medications or refer *Refer to Table 26, Page 61*
- Rule out MDD, GAD & Panic Disorder |

## TABLE 11: SUMMARY OF DIAGNOSIS AND CLASSIFICATION FOR BIPOLAR I AND II | SIGNS | CLASSIFY AS: | MANAGEMENT | | --- | --- | --- | | If the patient has:
A. Abnormally and persistent elevated, expansive or irritable mood and abnormally and persistently increase activity or energy lasting at least one week
B. \*\*PLUS\*\* 3 or more of the following;
- Flight of ideas
- Decreased need for sleep (feels rested after only three hours of sleep).
- More talkative than usual
- Inflated self-esteem or grandiosity
- Distractibility
- Increase in goal directed activity
- Excessive involvement in activities that have a high potential for painful consequences eg buying spree
C. Marked impairment in social and occupational functioning
D. Episodes not attributable to a physiological effect of a substance e.g. drugs, medications or other medical condition | BIPOLAR I DISORDER MANIC EPISODE | - Initiate the following medications or refer;
- Anti-psychotics *Check Table 30 & 31 Page 64*
\*\*PLUS\*\* a mood stabilizer *Refer page 69*
- \*\*PLUS\*\* a sedative if insomnia is one of the presenting symptom preferably Promethazine HCl 50mg to 75mg nocte for 7/7
- Psycho-education
- Adherence counseling *Refer page 81*
- Family involvement *Refer page 81*
- Counseling on alcohol and substance use issues |

text:
## TABLE 15: SUMMARY OF CLASSIFICATION AND MANAGEMENT OF NEUROCOGNITIVE DISORDERS | SIGNS | CLASSIFY AS: | MANAGEMENT | | --- | --- | --- | | If the patient has
• A disturbance in attention and awareness
• A disturbance develops over a short period of time and fluctuates in severity during the course of a day.
• \*\*PLUS\*\* disturbance in cognition (memory deficit, disorientation, language challenges etc.)
• Evidence from history, physical examination or laboratory findings that the disturbance is a direct physiological consequences of another medical condition | DELIRIUM |
• Initiate the following interventions or refer
• Manage the physical condition first
• \*\*PLUS\*\* a sedative preferably Lorazepam 0.5 to 1mg nocte for seven days if presents with insomnia
• Psycho-education
• Adherence counseling *Refer page 90*
• Family involvement *Refer page 81* | | The same symptoms as above but they are due to side effects of medications | MEDICATION INDUCED DELIRIUM | As above \*\*PLUS\*\* withdrawal the medication causing side effects | | If the patient has
• evidence of modest decline level of performance in one or more cognitive domains (attention, executive function, learning and memory, language, perceptual motor or social cognition)
• The cognitive deficit do not interfere with independence in everyday activities | MILD NEUROCOGNITIVE DISORDER | • As above for managing Major Neurocognitive Disorder |

Continued alcohol use despite having persistent or recurrent social or interpersonal problems caused or exacerbated by the effects of alcohol.

text:
## <u>TABLE 25: SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS</u> IN THE MANAGEMENT OF MAJOR DEPRESSIVE DISORDERS

| Special case | Intervention |
| --- | --- |
| If younger than 12 years | *• No antidepressants, provide counselling then refer* |
| Pregnant women and breastfeeding mothers | • Antidepressants should be avoided as far as possible and the refer |
| Depression with psychotic symptoms | • Prescribe anti-depressants + anti-psychotics |
| BAD, depressive phase. | • Prescribe mood stabilizer + anti-depressant + antipsychotic |
| If symptoms of mania emerge during treatment of depression | • Immediately stop antidepressants and refer |

heading_path: Chapter 5: Non Pharmacological Intervetions > Home Visits and Community Integration Job Aid > Guide for Interpreting PHQ-9 Scores
text:
## Guide for Interpreting PHQ-9 Scores

| Score | Recommended Actions |
| --- | --- |
| 0-4 | Normal range or full remission. The score suggests the patient may not need depression treatment. |
| 5-9 | Minimal depressive symptoms. Support, educate |
| 10-14 | Major depression, mild severity. Use clinical judgment about treatment, based on patient's duration of symptoms and functional impairment. Treat with antidepressant or psychotherapy. |
| 15-19 | Major depression, moderate severity. Warrants treatment for depression, using antidepressant, psychotherapy or a combination of treatment. |
| 20 or higher | Major depression, severe severity. Warrants treatment with antidepressant and psychotherapy, especially if not improved on monotherapy; follow frequently. |
